title: Digital Certificates, Digital Signatures, PKI & Key Management
description: How digital signatures and certificates work, how a PKI builds trust across untrusted networks, and how keys are managed through their lifecycle.

nodes.title: Digital Signatures
nodes.description:
Digital signatures provide three major services: integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.
They are used in many places:
- Email: verify the integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation of a message.
- Code signing: verify that an update you downloaded (for example, for an iPhone) really came from the vendor (Apple) and was not modified in transit.
- Legal documents such as PDFs: let others verify exactly who signed the document.

children.title: Integrity
children.description: You can tell whether a message or file has been changed or modified in any way.

children.title: Authenticity
children.description: You know who the message came from: who the sender is.

children.title: Non-repudiation
children.description:
Someone cannot deny the validity of something.
Digital signatures give non-repudiation in two scenarios: origin and delivery.

children.title: Origin
children.description: Non-repudiation of origin: the sender cannot deny that they sent exactly the message that was received.

children.title: Delivery
children.description: Non-repudiation of delivery: the receiver cannot deny that they received a specific message.

nodes.title: Digital Certificates
nodes.description:
Used to verify the owner of a public key.
To communicate securely with someone, you often need their public key and they need yours. If you just exchange public keys across the internet, anyone could intercept and modify them, or swap in their own key, and you would have no idea it happened.
Example: you cannot communicate securely with your online bank unless you know you have the bank's public key.

children.title: Verify the owner of a Public Key
children.description:
The core job of a digital certificate: bind a public key to a named identity, so you can trust whose key you have before you use it.
Two important pieces of information in a certificate are the name of the owner of the public key and a copy of their public key.

children.title: X.509
children.description:
Many different organizations can create digital certificates:
- A big Certificate Authority, such as Comodo, Symantec, DigiCert or Entrust: everyone in the world trusts the certificate.
- Your company: the certificate is trusted only within the company.
- You, with a self-signed certificate: no one but you trusts it.
Because certificates come from so many sources, a standard is needed to make them interoperable. That standard is X.509.

children.title: Replacement
children.description:
CAs issue each certificate for a limited period, often one year or less for public web certificates. The expiry date is written in the certificate itself.
When the expiry date is reached, or just before, a new certificate must be created. Replacement is this regular replacement of expired certificates, and the expiry date shows when it is due.

children.title: Revocation
children.description:
A certificate holds a copy of a public key. The matching private key must stay private: if it is compromised, no communication from that entity can be trusted.
If your private key is compromised, tell everyone at once not to trust your public key: ask your Certificate Authority to revoke your certificate. The CA keeps a list of all revoked certificates.
Before you trust the public key in any certificate, check with the CA that the certificate has not been revoked. If it has, do not trust the key.
Software such as a web browser checks for you with one of two protocols: CRL or OCSP.

children.title: CRL
children.description:
The older, less efficient way to check whether a certificate is revoked.
The client asks the CA whether a certificate is revoked. The CA sends a large file listing every certificate it has ever revoked, and the client searches the whole list for the certificate. Lots of overhead.
Full name: Certificate Revocation List.

children.title: OCSP
children.description:
The much newer and more efficient way to check whether a certificate is revoked.
The client asks the CA for the revocation status of one specific certificate, and the CA replies with that status: revoked, or good.
Full name: Online Certificate Status Protocol.

children.title: Pinning
children.description:
Certificate pinning. When you download a certificate from a server, there is a very small but non-zero chance that an attacker intercepts it and forwards a spoofed certificate. DigiNotar is a real-world example.
Instead, trust a local certificate pinned on your system. Less secure: pin the first certificate you receive from the server. More secure: use software that comes with pre-installed pinned certificates.
Significant issues have been found with pinning, and Certificate Transparency has superseded it. Know it in case it is on the exam.

nodes.title: PKI
nodes.description:
The broad set of roles, policies, procedures, hardware and software used to create, distribute, use, store, replace and revoke digital certificates.
Its purpose is to bind a public key to its owner, so you can trust users and systems you communicate with across an untrustworthy environment such as the internet.
Full name: Public Key Infrastructure.

children.title: Certificate Authority (Root of Trust)
children.description:
All trust in a PKI is ultimately rooted in the Certificate Authority, which is why it is called the root of trust.
The CA uses its private key to sign (encrypt) data that includes the owner's name and public key, creating a digital certificate. Only the CA has its private key, so no one can modify its certificates or create spoofed ones that look as if they came from it.
Anyone can verify (decrypt) a certificate from a big public CA, because everyone has the CA's public key: it comes pre-installed in browsers such as Firefox, Chrome and Safari.

children.title: Registration Authority
children.description:
Before a CA creates a certificate for you, it must proof your identity: confirm you are who you say you are.
The role within the CA that does this identity proofing is the Registration Authority.

children.title: Intermediate / Issuing CA
children.description:
If the CA signed new certificates directly with its root private key, that key would have to sit on a system connected to the internet. If the root private key is ever compromised, no certificate the CA has ever issued can be trusted.
So the root private key is kept offline and air-gapped, in a highly secure location.
The root key signs only the certificates of the CAs one level below it. Those CAs sign the next level down, and the lowest level signs the entity certificates customers pay a CA for. This is the chain of trust. You can follow it back up to verify that the CA's private key signed the first certificate in the chain.
Exam tip: the role in the CA that actually hands out certificates to customers is this one, not the root.

children.title: Certificate DB (Revocation List)
children.description: Each CA keeps its own Certificate DB: a list of every certificate it has ever issued, and which of them have been revoked.

children.title: Certificate Store (Local)
children.description:
Secure local storage on an end-point device, such as a desktop, laptop or mobile phone. It holds your private keys and any other keys and certificates you need, such as the big CAs' public keys.
Every end-point device has its own certificate store.

nodes.title: Key Management
nodes.description:
The hardest part of security is cryptography, and the hardest part of cryptography is key management.
Keys must be handled very securely in every key management activity: generation, distribution, storage, rotation, disposition and recovery.

children.title: Kerckhoffs's Principle
children.description:
Stated in 1883: a cryptosystem should be secure even if everything about the system, except the key, is public knowledge.
An attacker can know the algorithm and the initialization vector and have the ciphertext, and the data stays secure as long as the key is kept secret.
This is why keys must be generated, distributed, stored, rotated, disposed of and recovered very securely.

children.title: Generation
children.description:
Creating new symmetric keys or asymmetric key pairs.
Critical: each new key must be selected randomly from the entire keyspace, to avoid the plague of cryptography: patterns.

children.title: Distribution
children.description: Securely sending new keys to whoever needs them, and no one else.

children.title: Diffie-Hellman, Out-of-band, Hybrid
children.description:
Options for key distribution:
- Diffie-Hellman: a key exchange protocol that uses asymmetric techniques to generate the same key for two people without sending the key itself.
- Out-of-band: send the key through a different communication channel, such as a letter, a carrier pigeon, or a phone call where you read out 256 ones and zeros.
- Hybrid: more realistic and much more common. Encrypt the symmetric key with the recipient's public key (for example, Alice's) and send it. Only Alice can decrypt it, with her private key. Then switch to symmetric cryptography to encrypt and decrypt lots of data quickly and efficiently. It is called hybrid because asymmetric cryptography is used to send a symmetric key. TLS works this way: asymmetric cryptography sets up a symmetric session key.

children.title: Storage
children.description:
Created or received keys must be stored in an extremely secure location.
Two pieces of hardware are purpose-built to store encryption keys securely.

children.title: TPM, HSM
children.description:
- TPM: a tiny chip built into end-point devices such as desktops, laptops and mobile phones, designed to store encryption keys very securely. Whole drive encryption typically relies on a TPM to protect its key.
- HSM: typically an external, standalone device. It stores encryption keys securely and acts as a cryptographic accelerator, for example to encrypt, decrypt and verify digital signatures quickly and efficiently.
Full names: Trusted Platform Module; Hardware Security Module.

children.title: Rotation
children.description:
Change encryption keys periodically: rotate to a new symmetric key or asymmetric key pair.
How often depends on the value of the data being protected and the risk of the keys being compromised, among other factors.

children.title: Disposition
children.description: Sometimes every single copy of a key must be securely and defensibly destroyed.

children.title: Crypto-shredding, Key Destruction
children.description:
Destroy encrypted data by destroying every copy of the keys used to encrypt it. Both names describe the same technique, and it is one reason to destroy every copy of a key.
If the data was encrypted with an excellent algorithm such as AES and every copy of the key is destroyed, the data is unrecoverable, and so effectively destroyed.

children.title: Recovery
children.description: Sometimes a lost key must be recovered. There are a few ways to do it.

children.title: Split Knowledge, Dual Control, Key Escrow
children.description:
- Split Knowledge: no single person knows the whole key. Each of two or more people holds only a part, and to recover the key they must combine their parts.
- Dual Control: two or more people must perform an action together to recover the key. Think of launching a nuclear missile, where two people turn their keys at the same time.
- Key Escrow: a copy of the key is deposited with a trusted third party. To recover the key, ask the third party for its copy.
